Tyre Trace is a research workbench for tyre degradation, forecast uncertainty, and the next practice run. It connects measured race evidence to decisions, while keeping assumptions visible. The dashboard opens from saved results. It does not launch model fits or fetch new race data when a page opens.

Inside a stint, tyre wear and fuel burn follow the same clock. A lap-time slope alone cannot separate them. Pit stops reset tyre age while fuel keeps falling. Qualifying supplies a separate track-evolution anchor. We distinguish within-weekend compound contrasts from absolute degradation, which needs stronger transport assumptions.

The race explorer contains eighty-four cached weekends. Choose a driver and inspect measured lap times, timing-derived traffic, and tyre stints. The physical-compound lookup uses dated supplier or Formula One sources. Unresolved compounds remain unknown, rather than silently inheriting a placeholder. Tables and complete data exports accompany the plots.

Qualifying estimates how track pace changes over the session. The intervals here describe parameters, rather than future race laps. Carrying qualifying evolution into a race remains an assumption, with its own estimated scaling. Every tyre nomination has a season, an event, a date, and a primary-source link.

Complexity has to earn its place. We compare probabilistic forecasts using the continuous ranked probability score, with a separate ninety-percent coverage gate. Robust practice slopes and a regime model were implemented and evaluated. They did not earn adoption on the current data. Gradient boosting is a serious challenger. We preserve its strong results, the uncertainty across weekends, and sampler-convergence diagnostics.

These forecasts use earlier race history, current practice, qualifying, and five opening green race laps per driver. The shaded band describes an individual future lap time. It does not validate a joint race trajectory or a hidden tyre-wear parameter. Tyre strategy and race distance are conditioned inputs. Change the driver or method to inspect the evidence directly.

All four baseline families are compared on the same laps. The main uncertainty result uses retrospectively filtered stints. Removing that pace filter gives undercoverage, so broader forecasting is not validated. Austin is a separate unseen offline holdout, frozen before timing access. The preselected ML model fails its criterion; we retain the result without retuning. One weekend cannot establish prospective replication. Strategy diagnostics use a fitted reference, not observed counterfactual truth.

The run planner designs a practice programme for information under operating constraints. Change the available time, tyres, and programme options to inspect the trade-offs. The mathematical planner is tested in Python and TypeScript. A counterfactual benefit in the game still requires executing the proposed programme and a matched conventional programme under controlled conditions.

The game can expose fuel mass and wear at each wheel. The recording workflow preserves raw UDP evidence, checks packet layouts and integrity, and supports deterministic replay. The example shown is synthetic. Actual game validation requires the live self-check and a controlled capture with a pit stop. Reading truth channels does not prove that an estimator inferred them.

The software, comparisons, and evidence are ready to inspect. Negative findings remain visible. The next human steps are the live game experiment, final review, and submission. Future-race replication and latent-state recovery remain separate scientific questions.
